what: Reynolds Consumer Products makes household goods. Its best-known product is Reynolds Wrap aluminium foil; it also owns Hefty bags and containers, and makes disposable plates, cups, cutlery and food storage bags, including the own-brand versions supermarkets sell beside them.
customers: American households, reached through supermarkets, warehouse clubs, discounters and online retailers. It also manufactures the store-brand equivalents for those same retailers.
money: Aluminium foil, parchment, baking cups and oven bags.
Rubbish bags, food storage bags and containers.
Disposable plates, cups and cutlery, plus own-brand products made for retailers.
moat: Reynolds Wrap is one of the few genuinely dominant brands in a commodity product: most people do not know another foil brand, and that recognition commands shelf space and a price premium over an identical own-brand product. Making the store brands too is a shrewd position — Reynolds earns either way, and it keeps a rival manufacturer off the shelf.
risks: Revenue has been flat at about $3.7B to $3.8B for four years, so there is no growth to speak of.
Aluminium and resin prices are the main input costs, and they move independently of what the company can charge.
Own-brand products take share from branded ones when household budgets tighten, and that trend has been running.
Debt of $1.7B against $147.0M of cash is meaningful for a business with flat revenue.
Seven analysts average a $27.00 target, about 10% above the current price.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 15.9 times earnings, 10.6 times EV/EBITDA and 18.4 times free cash flow.
Reynolds Wrap has brand recognition in a commodity category, which is rare and supports a price premium.
Making the retailers’ own-brand versions means Reynolds captures the trade-down rather than losing to it.
Household staples demand is almost entirely non-cyclical: people buy foil and bin bags in every economy.
Free cash flow of $281.0M supports a substantial dividend.
watch: Volume growth separately from pricing, and the branded share against own-brand. Flat revenue could be falling volumes offset by price increases, which is a different business from stable volumes.
view: Reynolds owns one of the strangest competitive positions in consumer goods: a dominant brand in a product that is physically identical whoever makes it. Aluminium foil is aluminium foil. And yet most Americans reach for Reynolds Wrap without considering alternatives, and pay a premium over the own-brand roll sitting next to it. That recognition, built over decades, is the entire asset.

What makes the position cleverer than it first appears is that Reynolds also manufactures those own-brand rolls for the supermarkets. So when a household trades down to save money, Reynolds still makes the product — at a lower margin, but it captures the trade-down rather than losing it to a competitor. It also means no rival manufacturer gets a foothold on the shelf. That is a genuinely well-constructed defensive position.

The business characteristics are otherwise those of a mature staple: demand that does not care about the economy, revenue flat at about $3.7 billion for four years, and input costs — aluminium and plastic resin — that move independently of what the company can charge. The margin therefore swings with commodity prices rather than with anything management does, which is why a strong brand in this category earns an 8% net margin rather than something better.

At 15.9 times earnings and 10.6 times EV/EBITDA with $1.7 billion of debt, this is fairly priced for what it is: a no-growth staple with a good brand, generating $281 million of free cash flow to support the dividend. The question I would want answered is whether the flat revenue is stable volumes with flat pricing or falling volumes offset by price increases — those are very different businesses, and the consolidated revenue line hides which one you own.
bull: Brand recognition holds the price premium while the own-brand manufacturing captures any trade-down, and non-cyclical demand funds the dividend reliably.
bear: Own-brand share keeps rising at the expense of margin, commodity input costs squeeze a thin 8% margin, and flat revenue meets $1.7 billion of debt.
